Decided by Mark 2026-09-15 and implemented in 4632471: the SECOND instance refuses; the running daemon is never touched. Detection is an exclusive non-blocking flock, chosen over a connect() probe (which races -- two daemons starting together both probe, both find nothing, both bind) and over documenting the takeover (which cannot even warn accurately, since without a liveness check you never learn you displaced anyone).

Why flock is the right primitive and not just a mechanism: the kernel releases it when its holder dies, so it answers exactly the question the socket path cannot -- is the daemon that made this still alive? A crashed daemon's lock is already free, so stale-socket cleanup keeps working unchanged.

Details worth keeping:
- The lock is taken BEFORE the unlink. After it would be pointless.
- The lock is keyed to the socket path (<socket>.lock), NOT its directory. A directory-wide lock breaks the integration tests, which bind a dozen sockets under /tmp, and the real invariant is one daemon per socket anyway.
- The lock file is never unlinked. Removing it races a process that has already opened the same path and would leave it locking an unlinked inode.
- The refused instance exits non-zero with the message on stderr, matching the settled rule for a command that did no work.
- No new dependency: libc was already a persona-grpc dependency. flock(2) exists on Darwin too, so the shipped LaunchAgent is covered.

Verified with real processes, not only unit tests: a second personad exits 1 with 'another personad is already serving <path>' while the first keeps serving with its socket intact; a clean exit is reclaimed; and a SIGKILLed daemon that leaves BOTH socket and lock behind is also reclaimed, because the kernel released the flock. Five mutations verified, including the naive wrong fix (refuse whenever the socket file exists), which the reclaim-after-crash test catches.

Follow-on note, not acted on: systemd Restart=on-failure would restart a refused instance every 5s. A user unit is a singleton so systemd will not double-start it; the realistic collision is a hand-run daemon, which simply prints and exits. If a hand-run daemon ever holds the socket while the unit starts, the unit restart-loops -- arguably the correct alarm, but RestartPreventExitStatus= is there if that proves annoying.
